activities.anchor: Data moves in characteristic patterns, and each exposes a different attack surface
activities.caption: file each channel by its direction
activities.name: cryptoDirectionSort

config.prompt: File each channel by its direction:
buckets: both ways, one at a time
config.why: Mode and timing expose their own weaknesses — serial, parallel, asynchronous, synchronous, packet-switched: each is a different door.

activities.anchor: Cosmic rays, cable noise and buffer bugs corrupt data constantly
activities.caption: pair each code with what it guarantees
activities.name: cryptoCodeMatch

config.prompt: Pair each code with what it guarantees:

pairs.right: catches any single-bit flip, misses any even number of them
better than parity, but reordering two words slips through
catches all burst errors of 32 bits or fewer and all odd numbers of bit flips
detects up to d − 1 flips, corrects up to ⌊(d − 1)/2⌋

config.why: Parity guards memory buses, CRC guards Ethernet frames and ZIP files, Reed–Solomon still talks to Voyager — but none of them catches an adversary, only accidents.

activities.anchor: Confusing the two has shipped broken protocols
activities.caption: drag the divider across the check field
activities.name: cryptoTamperCompare

config.prompt: Two ways to guard a message — drag the divider:

before.label: unkeyed code (CRC)
before.text: Recomputable by anyone: a man-in-the-middle edits the message and its check field in one step — it detects accidents, not adversaries.

after.label: keyed construction (MAC)
after.text: A hash seeded with a secret key — the attacker cannot recompute the tag, so edits are caught.

config.why: Guarding against accidents is arithmetic; guarding against intention is cryptography — and mixing them has sunk real systems.

activities.anchor: Its security budget is the keyspace
activities.caption: call the brute-force bill
activities.name: cryptoKeysEst

config.prompt: A 128-bit block cipher's key count is ≈ 3.4 × 10³⁸. At a trillion guesses per second, roughly how long to try them all?
config.why: About 10¹⁹ years — a billionfold the universe's age. The dangers are elsewhere: botched wiring, repeated nonces, and getting the secret to the other party.
config.context: Keyspace strength is the budget; distribution and wiring are where systems actually die.

activities.anchor: It does nothing about the endpoints
activities.caption: true or false — what the cipher promises
activities.name: cryptoSafeJudge

statements.s: Encryption makes data safe, full stop.
statements.why: It protects one state — on the wire or at rest; nothing about the two ends, stolen passwords, misconfigured databases, insiders, or the pasted-into-chat case.

statements.s: Threat modelling starts where the cipher ends.
statements.why: The two ends still see the secret in the clear — the maths is one layer of the trust machine.

statements.s: Encryption at rest also protects data while an employee has it open on screen.
statements.why: The ends see the secret in the clear — encryption guards states, not every moment of its life.

statements.s: TLS on the wire and disk encryption are the same guarantee.
statements.why: Different states, different mechanisms — 'safe' is always safe-against-what-and-when.

activities.anchor: generates a fresh key for every session and erases it
activities.caption: walk the stolen-key scenario
activities.name: cryptoEphemeralBranch

config.root: An attacker records all of today's encrypted traffic and, next year, steals the server's long-term secret. Walk the design question.

start.text: With static agreement, what can the attacker now do?

choices.label: Decrypt everything recorded last week
choices.feedback: Exactly the failure forward secrecy exists to prevent — today's capture becomes next year's plaintext.

choices.label: Nothing — the maths still holds
choices.feedback: Only if the sessions were ephemeral: per-connection secrets, erased after use.

ok.text: With ephemeral Diffie–Hellman (the E in DHE/ECDHE), what does the stolen long-term secret buy?

choices.label: Impersonation going forward — but not decryption of the past
choices.feedback: Those per-connection secrets no longer exist anywhere: steal today's material, still cannot open last week's recording.

choices.label: Full decryption of history
choices.feedback: That is the static world — which is why 'rotate your keys' is a design property, not a policy slogan.

static.text: Static agreement turns next year's theft into last week's plaintext — the case that motivated ephemeral keys.

fail.text: Full history decryption is exactly what forward secrecy denies — Signal's double ratchet goes further, re-deriving per message.

forward.text: Forward secrecy: the stolen long-term secret buys impersonation going forward, but yesterday's capture stays closed.

config.why: Ephemeral per-connection secrets mean even a later server compromise cannot open yesterday's capture.

activities.anchor: the guarantee is conditional but precise
activities.caption: fill the blanks — the one cipher with perfect secrecy
activities.name: cryptoPadCloze

config.text: Shannon's one-time pad (secret as long as the %%0%%, used once) is the only cipher with perfect secrecy — the ciphertext leaks literally %%1%% information — and its impracticality motivates the modern standard: %%2%%, where breaking the scheme would solve a stated hard problem.
config.hint: Kerckhoffs's principle remains the foundation: assume the enemy knows the system; secrecy lives in the key alone.

activities.anchor: The migration is the rare engineering project whose deadline is defined by an adversary's hardware roadmap
activities.caption: slide to the standardisation year
activities.name: cryptoPqPlace

config.prompt: The quantum deadline: slide the marker to the year the first post-quantum algorithms were standardised.
config.why: 2024 — ML-KEM for key exchange and ML-DSA for signatures, built on lattice problems with no known quantum attack; Chrome and Signal already negotiate hybrid handshakes. Traffic captured today could be opened in 2035.
